questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A village memorial after the frontier was drawn
questions.learningObjective: Explain why official and local versions of the frontier differ.
questions.stem: A member's revision card compares the official line of settlement with what residents of the village remembered about the years before it.

answer.exemplar: The official account was a line drawn on a map by officials, marking how far settlement had reached, and it carried a single date at which the distinction ceased. The local version was a body of memories of hardship and arrival, in which the frontier was a condition people had lived through rather than a line on a map. The difference is therefore between a boundary that can be surveyed and an experience that belongs to the people who remember it, and a memorial is a way of keeping the second kind in public view.

questions.explanation: The official line was a surveyed boundary with a closing date, while the local version was a remembered experience of arrival and hardship. A memorial keeps the second in public view.
questions.hint: One is a boundary on a map and one is a memory of people.

questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about a village's frontier claim from a local history.

stimulus.body: The county paper of 1904 noted that the town had kept up a celebration each year of the day on which the first train arrived, and that the schoolchildren were marched out to the siding to see the engine come in. In 1931 the council replaced the celebration with a stone, and the inscription speaks of the founders as having crossed the frontier and made the town what it is. Nobody in the council could say where the phrase had come from, but everyone agreed it was not the phrase the first train used.

options.text: The memorial was built to dispute the census's finding that the frontier had closed
options.misconception: Makes the stone an instrument against the census

questions.explanation: A festival marking the first train became a stone describing founders who crossed a frontier, and no one could trace the phrase. The claim grew out of the festival.
questions.hint: Compare the 1904 celebration with what the 1931 stone says.

questions.topic: A village memorial after the frontier was drawn

stimulus.body: The group argued about the phrase on the stone. The census language was about population density and was written by officials in Washington who never saw the town. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two defects of the international league
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the two defects of the league worked together.
questions.stem: The group's notes on the league list two defects and give a worked example of each.

answer.exemplar: The league could not enforce a decision because it had no force of its own and no military to call on, so a state that refused to accept a resolution simply carried on. It could not even reach a resolution in the ordinary case, because the rule of unanimity meant that any state the council wished to condemn had a vote against its own condemnation. The example is instructive because the two defects were not independent: a rule that made action hard would have mattered little if the league had been able to act, and an enforcement power would have mattered little if the necessary agreement could never be reached.

questions.explanation: Unanimity made the decision hard to reach and the league had no means of enforcing one, so the two defects compounded each other and were not independent.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if only one defect had been present.

questions.topic: Two defects of the international league
questions.learningObjective: Conclude what a case summary shows about the league's machinery.

stimulus.body: The council was asked to condemn a state that had already acted. Its members could not agree, because the state that had acted was one of the permanent members whose consent was needed for anything the council did. The commission that looked into the matter reported that the state had gone beyond its rights, and the report was read, discussed and referred to a committee, and no measure followed. The group noted that the machinery was not at fault: every step in it had been performed.

options.text: The league could have acted on the report if the report had been more strongly worded
options.misconception: Assumes the wording of a report could have decided the vote

questions.explanation: Every step of the machinery was performed and the report was made, yet no measure followed, because the rules gave the accused state a veto. The defect was in the rules.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two defects of the international league
questions.learningObjective: Identify the point made by a member's summary card.

stimulus.body: Ask yourself why the league had a general assembly at all if the council did the work. The answer is that the assembly was the revolutionary part: every state, small ones included, had a vote and a public platform, and the argument for the whole institution was that a state's conduct could be named before the world. What the assembly could not do was take a decision against a state with a friend on the council, and it could not make any of that stick by itself. So the league's two faces have to be held together: an open public place, and an instrument that could not act.

questions.stem: The member's card is being discussed by the group. Which point about the league does the card make?

options.text: The league's public forum and its inability to enforce decisions are two sides of one institution
The assembly was the league's weakness, and the council was the part that really mattered
options.misconception: Ranks the two parts without the card's argument

options.text: The league was created for publicity, and enforcement was never seriously raised
options.misconception: Reduces the institution to publicity

options.text: The league's two faces show that the institution was never coherently designed at all
options.misconception: Misses that the card holds the two faces together

questions.explanation: The card argues that the assembly's public platform and the council's inability to act were two aspects of one institution, not defects to be ranked against each other.
questions.hint: The card's last sentence joins the two faces together.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Paying in goods and the price clause
questions.learningObjective: Establish what a source extract shows about the price clause.

stimulus.kind: extract from the group's source booklet
stimulus.body: Under the transfer agreement the German government might deliver goods and services instead of money, and the deliveries would be valued at prices fixed in the agreement. The prices were maxima, and the delivery of a consignment at a price below the maximum was not permitted, so that the German government could not enter the world market below the level set for it. The group noted that the prices in the agreement were set at the level of the years before the war, when German goods had cost more to make than they afterwards cost.

questions.stem: The extracts are read aloud, and the group is asked what the price clause shows. Which statement is supported?

options.text: It fixed maximum values for deliveries in kind, and set them above the current level of cost
It allowed the German government to value its own deliveries at whatever the market paid
options.misconception: Reverses the maxima into a minimum, and the valuation too

options.text: It required the German government to deliver goods at prices set by the creditors each quarter
options.misconception: Turns fixed maxima into a quarterly price set by creditors

options.text: It removed the question of price by crediting deliveries at their cost of production
options.misconception: Finds an exemption from valuation the text does not grant

questions.explanation: The prices were maxima fixed at pre-war levels, above the reduced cost of making German goods after the war, and no consignment could be delivered below them.
questions.hint: Note what the prices were and what they were set at.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Paying in goods and the price clause
questions.learningObjective: Identify the point a member's note makes about paying in goods.

stimulus.body: The clause is always described as a price clause, and people imagine a fixed price for German coal, but that is only the half of it. The other half is the account, because a delivery is not a payment until the committee has accepted the valuation and written it off against the sum owed. And the deliveries were things people wanted: bricks, timber, dyes, and a great deal of coal. Our own coal men were not sorry to see the prices fixed at the level I have just described.

questions.stem: The member's note is being read. Which point about paying in goods does it make?

options.text: Deliveries in kind were credited only after valuation, and the fixed prices helped foreign producers
Deliveries in kind were credited at once, and the fixed prices were set to help German producers
options.misconception: Reverses the credit procedure and the effect of the prices

options.text: Deliveries in kind replaced cash payments entirely once the price clause was agreed
options.misconception: Claims a total replacement the arrangements did not achieve

options.text: Deliveries in kind were made in goods the German government had no use for and did not want
options.misconception: Contradicts the list of wanted goods in the note

questions.explanation: A delivery was not a payment until its valuation was accepted and written off, and the fixed prices let foreign producers sell into a German market below their own cost.
questions.hint: The note says the coal men were pleased with the prices.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Paying in goods and the price clause
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a debtor's preference for goods reveals about a settlement.
questions.stem: The group's revision note asks what a debtor's preference for paying in goods tells you about a settlement built on payments.

answer.exemplar: A debtor who prefers to deliver goods rather than money is signalling that the goods can be sold abroad at a price fixed above what it costs to make them, so the transfer of the obligation becomes a subsidy to that trade and a transfer of the burden onto the industries of the creditors. What the preference does not tell you is anything about the size of the sum itself, because the terms of the settlement and the price of the goods in the outside market may both have changed since the schedule was agreed.

questions.explanation: A preference for goods means deliveries can be sold at fixed prices above cost, which subsidises the debtor's export trade at the creditors' expense. It says nothing about the sum.
questions.hint: Ask what the debtor gains by delivering rather than paying.

questions.learningObjective: Conclude which reading of the failures a source extract supports.

stimulus.kind: extract from the group's source booklet
stimulus.body: The bank of a market town with a population of four thousand failed in the autumn of 1930. Its assets were chiefly a single loan to the local woollen mill, the mill had failed to place its orders in the spring, and the directors had allowed the loan to grow for two years without new security. The town had no other bank of any size, and the depositors, who were mostly shopkeepers and farmers, were paid at sixty cents in the dollar over eighteen months. The group noted that a correspondent bank in the next county was also in the same condition, and that the two had lent to the same mill.

questions.stem: The group is asked which reading of the failures this extract supports.

options.text: A local concentration of lending that spread because two banks had backed the same industry
A collapse of confidence in banking that had no connection with how the banks were run
options.misconception: Finds a general panic where the extract shows the lending

options.text: A shortage of cash in the country, which forced sound banks to fail as well
options.misconception: Replaces the local cause with a national shortage of cash

options.text: A failure of the woollen trade that ruined every bank in the region alike
options.misconception: Generalises from one industry to every bank in the region

questions.explanation: Both banks had concentrated on the same mill, and the town's only bank failing left depositors with nowhere to go, so local concentration produced a wider collapse.
questions.hint: Notice the correspondent bank and the shared loan.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two readings of the bank failures
questions.learningObjective: Assess the conclusion the group reaches about the two readings.

stimulus.body: Half the group wanted the story to be about the system: banks lent their customers' savings to a handful of local trades, there was no pool of reserves anywhere, and when one bank closed the next one lost the deposits it had left. The other half wanted the story to be about the men: directors lent to their own friends, and a good many of them were crooked. The group split the difference in a way that was unsatisfactory, because a reform that puts the whole weight on the men leaves the structure exactly as it was, and a reform that only changes the structure leaves the same men in charge of the next bank.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the bank failures do these notes support?

options.text: The two readings are not alternatives, since fixing one leaves the other problem untouched
The two readings are alternatives, and the group had to choose between them on the evidence
options.misconception: Treats the two explanations as rival, not complementary

options.text: The system was sound and the failures were the work of a few dishonest directors
options.misconception: Settles for one half of the group's argument

options.text: The failures were the work of dishonest directors, and the structure was the real safeguard
options.misconception: Reverses the relation between the two explanations

questions.explanation: The notes argue that a reform aimed only at the men leaves the structure untouched, and one aimed only at the structure leaves the same men in charge of the next bank.
questions.hint: Read the last sentence about what each reform leaves behind.

questions.topic: Two readings of the bank failures
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of two failures shows about the readings.
questions.stem: A member's note compares the failure of a small market-town bank with the run on a large city bank that the public knew about.

answer.exemplar: The city bank failed because the public believed it would fail, which is the panic reading, while the market-town bank failed because one industry in one town stopped paying, which is the concentration reading. Together they show that the two are not rival stories but a chain, in which a local loss weakened a bank, the loss of confidence in that bank spread to others, and a fear of general collapse emptied the strongest institutions. Reform had to touch the structure and the standards, not one or the other.

questions.explanation: The city bank failed on fear and the market-town bank on a concentrated loan, so the two readings are stages of one chain rather than rival stories.
questions.hint: The two failures are consecutive, not competing.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A village memorial after the frontier was drawn
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the same fact served two different purposes.
questions.stem: A member's card compares the phrase on the stone with the phrase used in the census report of 1890.

answer.exemplar: The census phrase was a description of where settlement had reached, made for a statistical purpose and applied to the whole country at once. The phrase on the stone was a claim about what a particular village had been and had made of itself, addressed to anyone who came after. The same set of facts therefore served two different purposes, one administrative and one civic, and the village chose the civic use because the administrative use had already been made of the facts by others.

questions.explanation: The census phrase was an administrative description applied nationally, while the stone's phrase was a local claim of origin addressed to later generations.
questions.hint: One phrase was for officials and one for the town's readers.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A village memorial after the frontier was drawn
questions.learningObjective: Assess the compromise a study group reached about a memorial.

stimulus.body: The group spent most of its time on one question: whether a town that had been counted as frontier after the line was drawn was lying about itself. Two members said that the census had settled the matter and that the stone was a small vanity. The other two said the census had counted people, not memories, and that a community could remember a beginning long after the officials had closed the category. The notes end with a compromise: the question is not whether the town was on the frontier but which frontier it meant.

questions.stem: The revised notes end in a compromise. Which reading of the compromise does the group reach?

questions.explanation: The compromise distinguishes the frontier the census counted from the frontier the community remembered, so each answers its own question and neither is false.
questions.hint: Read the last sentence of the notes closely.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two defects of the international league
questions.learningObjective: Explain the argument for keeping the league's assembly.
questions.stem: The group's notes discuss why the league's assembly was kept even though it could not enforce anything.

answer.exemplar: The argument was that the league was meant to make the conduct of states a matter of public argument, so that a state accused before the assembly could not conduct its case in private, and the pressure of being named before the world would itself restrain it. The argument does not claim that such pressure would stop a great power, since the assembly had no means of enforcing its conclusions, and its defenders knew that a state which chose to ignore the league could do so at the cost of its reputation alone.

questions.explanation: The assembly was kept to make the conduct of states a matter of public argument, and the pressure of being named was expected to restrain a state without enforcement.
questions.hint: What was the assembly for, if not for compelling?
